content: About us Membership Contact us Sun October 4, 2026 Home Society Economy Politics Sports Culture International Multimedia Tourism Iran, WHO join efforts to eliminate human rabies by 2030 Society September 29, 2026 - 15:37 TEHRAN – The National Plan for the Elimination of Human Rabies 2026–2030 was formally countersigned at a seminar marking World Rabies Day, hosted by the Ministry of Health and Medical Education's Centre for Communicable Disease Control. The initiative aims to strengthen national efforts to prevent and ultimately eliminate human rabies through coordinated measures in disease surveillance, prevention, public awareness, and timely access to post-exposure treatment. Speaking at the event, Dr Jean Jabbour, WHO Representative in the Islamic Republic of Iran, emphasized the need for collaboration across human health, veterinary services, municipalities, communities and other sectors through a One Health approach. He also highlighted timely care after animal bites and dog vaccination as essential measures to prevent rabies deaths Achieving the goal of zero human deaths from rabies by 2030 requires enhancing collaborations among the health system, veterinary, municipalities, and local communities within the framework of the “One Health” approach, Jabbour stated. Dog bites contribute to 99 percent of human rabies cases. Despite being fatal, rabies is entirely preventable. However, no single organization can defeat the disease on its own, the health ministry’s website quoted Jabbour as saying. The official made the remarks on the occasion of World Rabies Day, which is marked on September 28 every year. Highlighting this year’s World Rabies Day theme, ‘Stronger Together’, he noted that rabies elimination needs ongoing multi-sectoral cooperation among physicians, veterinarians, health staff, municipalities, and local communities. Referring to the number of animal bites in the country, he said over the past two decades there has been a fivefold increase in the number of reported cases. More than 441,000 individuals bitten by animals were referred to medical centers in the past Iranian year (March 2025 – March 2026). Twenty of them lost their lives, and it could have been prevented. Eleven individuals died without receiving any treatment. The statistics indicate that, in addition to prompt presentation of the bitten person to medical centers, timely and appropriate post-exposure care and the raise of public awareness are critical, and every case of animal bite must be treated as a medical emergency. When a person is bitten or scratched by an animal, even if the bite looks small, they have to visit a healthcare provider right away, he added. Noting that approximately four out of every five confirmed rabies deaths in Iran are due to dog bites, Jabbour stated that stray dogs alone account for more than half of these cases, while the rest are attributed to wild animals, including wolves and foxes. The official underlined the role of One Health strategies for rabies control, including constant vaccination of dogs, effective management of stray dogs, and the promotion of close cooperation among the human health, environmental health, and veterinary sectors, he added. Lauding the adopted measures in the country, Jabbour said some 729 rabies prevention and treatment centers are operating across the country, and post-exposure care services are provided in all provinces. Around one million doses of human rabies vaccine and 180,000 vials of anti-rabies serum are procured for the national program, annually; Pasteur Institute of Iran helps diagnose confirmed cases of rabies as well as train physicians and health workers. The official went on to say that the development of a national strategic document for rabies eradication is also a significant step toward aligning Iran with the global goal of “zero human deaths from dog-mediated rabies by 2030”, adding that the WHO is committed to supporting Iran, through technical assistance and collaboration, in achieving the goal. Why “Stronger Together”? The 2026 theme, ‘Stronger Together’, highlights a simple truth: rabies elimination is only possible when we work together. Expand access to life-saving dog vaccinations. Improve rabies surveillance and reporting systems. Strengthen public awareness and education. Support policies that protect both people and animals. Build sustainable community-led solutions. Rabies elimination depends on connected systems. Stronger partnerships create stronger outcomes! We all have a role to play From local communities and veterinary professionals to governments, healthcare workers, educators, and global partners, we all have role to play in making a world free from rabies a reality. Communities: Communities are often the first line of defense against rabies. Education, awareness, and responsible animal care help prevent cases before they happen. Veterinary Professionals: Mass dog vaccination remains the most effective way to stop rabies at its source. Healthcare Workers: Timely treatment and accurate diagnosis save lives. Governments and Policymakers: Strong legislation, investment, and national coordination are essential for long-term progress. Global Partners: Collaboration across sectors helps share resources, expertise, and solutions that accelerate impact. One Health in action Rabies elimination depends on interconnected action. Education, vaccination, surveillance, and legislation cannot work in isolation, they must function as part of one coordinated system. World Rabies Day 2026 reinforces the importance of a One Health approach, recognizing the connection between human, animal, and environmental health. content: Skip to contentMenuToday's paper Long IslandSportsNewsInvestigationsRestaurantsOpinionBusinessThings to DoSchoolsObitsNewsday TVSearchTOGETHER LI HealthYankees in ALDSHalloween events on LITop 50 best restaurantsWallet Watch NewsHealthOnly in Newsday Rabies is spreading in LI's raccoons, and workers are responding with vaccine bait A raccoon at an undisclosed Suffolk County location feeds on oral rabies vaccine bait. Credit: Suffolk County Department of Health Services By Lisa L. Colangelolisa.colangelo@newsday.com@lisalcolangeloUpdated October 3, 2026 5:22 pm Share Raccoons will eat just about anything, especially if it's covered with cod liver oil and fish meal crumbles. That’s what health officials on Long Island are hoping, as workers distribute hundreds of thousands of fish-flavored packets containing rabies vaccine in wooded areas, culverts and other places raccoons like to gather. Vaccine baiting for raccoons is an important weapon against a wildlife rabies outbreak that started in Nassau County in 2024 and spread into Suffolk County last year. Since February 2025, 51 cases of terrestrial rabies have been documented in Suffolk County — in 49 raccoons and two cats. Before that, there had not been a case since 2009, officials said. Terrestrial rabies cases do not include bats, which also carry the virus. WHAT NEWSDAY FOUND The local outbreak of terrestrial wildlife rabies on Long Island, which includes raccoons and some cats, has been moving farther into Suffolk County in recent months. Health officials are placing rabies vaccine baits, flavored with fish, to attract raccoons. Once they bite the bait, the vaccine will enter their system and provide protection from the virus. Residents are warned to stay away from wildlife and make sure their pets have updated rabies vaccines. Pets are an important barrier between the virus in wildlife and people. Oral rabies vaccine baits, covered in cod liver oil and other substances, that were distributed by the Nassau County Department of Health. Credit: Credit: Nassau County Department of Health Most of the cases were clustered in Amityville, with a few in Lindenhurst, Deer Park and Wyandanch. But over the past few months, they also have been found farther east and north in Babylon, Bay Shore, Islip, Northport, Smithtown and Kings Park. Sign up By clicking Sign up, you agree to our privacy policy. A raccoon picked up in Manorville in June after an encounter with a local resident tested positive for rabies. Health officials believe it likely was relocated from another area since its location was far from where other raccoons with rabies were found. Preventive measures With surveillance, vaccine baits and free rabies shots for pets, Suffolk County is trying to hold the line. Rabies is a potentially deadly virus that is transmitted via the saliva of an infected animal. That can happen through a bite or by the infected saliva getting into an open wound, eyes, nose or mouth, according to the state Health Department. While fatal human cases of rabies are rare — the last one in New York State was more than 30 years ago and involved an encounter with a bat — they also can be avoided with prompt medical treatment. Suffolk County already has distributed about 240,000 vaccine bait packets, and Nassau will put out more than 144,000 by Oct. 9. “The goal of the bait program is to provide herd immunity,” said Dr. Meghan Davis, a veterinarian and chair of the master of public health program at Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. “But you are not going to catch every member of the herd. ... It’s about serving as a line of defense.” The vaccine baits are making a difference, Suffolk County Health Commissioner Dr. Gregson Pigott told Newsday. He said U.S. Department of Agriculture staff trapped and tested blood from numerous raccoons in the areas that were baited last year to determine the effectiveness of the program. The tests showed 26% of raccoons showed an antibody response, above the average of 10%-15% that the USDA typically finds following a first-time baiting program. Staying away from wildlife is the best way to avoid any kind of illness, state officials said, advising people to contact a rehabilitator if they believe an animal is sick or injured. If a person or pet is in contact with or bitten by a wild animal, they should seek immediate medical treatment and contact their county's health department. Companion dogs, cats and ferrets must be vaccinated against rabies under New York State law, the first shot no later than four months after birth and the second within a year later. Booster shots are required at different intervals, one year or three years, depending on the animal and vaccine. Vaccinating pets Davis pointed out that while the baiting program is designed to reduce how many wild animals become rabid and infectious, dog and cat vaccines protect people by providing a shield for the animals most likely to infect them. “Especially if you live on Long Island,” said Dr. Carly Fox, senior veterinarian for urgent and emergency care at the Schwarzman Animal Medical Center in Manhattan. “If you let your dog outside or if you have a cat that goes outside, they can experience interactions with wildlife that you just don't witness.” In two separate Kings Park incidents, dogs and their owners came in contact with raccoons that later tested positive for rabies. The dogs had been previously vaccinated against rabies and received booster shots. The individuals were treated for exposure. Both counties have held several free rabies vaccination clinics for pets since the first cases of the local outbreak were discovered in Nassau County in 2024. The cases included four raccoons and two stray cats. A Suffolk County Department of Health Services employee distributes vaccine baits in Suffolk County last month. Credit: Suffolk County Department of Hea In early 2025, as cases started to rise, Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman suggested raccoons with rabies may have crossed over from Queens because New York City did not perform rabies vaccine baiting in 2024. The city Health Department said it didn't have the funding that year to continue the program but also said there is no way to determine "how and where rabid raccoons are moving or being moved by people." It also pointed out there was rabies vaccine distribution in southwestern Nassau County in September 2024. Nassau and Suffolk started active surveillance programs, testing raccoons that were found dead or appeared sickly or disoriented. Since raccoons have acclimated well to urban and suburban environments, seeing them during the day foraging for food is common and not a sign they are ill. The number of terrestrial wildlife rabies cases in Nassau jumped to 27 in 2025 — 26 raccoons and one stray cat — and has dropped to one raccoon so far this year. In a statement announcing the latest round of baiting, Nassau Health Commissioner Dr. Irina Gelman called the decline in confirmed rabies cases “encouraging.” “Following the return of rabies in 2024, NCDOH implemented extensive rabies control efforts, including an expanded oral rabies vaccine baiting program to help vaccinate raccoons and other terrestrial wildlife against the virus,” she said. “Those highly successful efforts have continued.” Occasional outbreaks These local outbreaks generally last from one to two years, followed by a decline in the raccoon population due to deaths from the virus, the state Health Department said. The population rebounds in about five years, sometimes causing “periodic flare-ups” of rabies. The dynamics of exposure between humans and raccoons are changing and becoming more challenging, especially with people who feed colonies of stray cats every day, said Gary Whittaker, a professor of virology at the Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine. Those caretakers are in contact with cats that sometimes end up sharing resources with raccoons — putting them at risk of contracting rabies, he said. “People want to take care of the cats and they put out food for the cats, and the raccoons are taking advantage of that,” he said. “It’s also allowing an increase in the raccoon population.” Whittaker was one of the authors of a study that examined how raccoons in Brooklyn's Green-Wood Cemetery acclimate to the environment and interact with other animals. “They are incredibly successful, smart animals,” he said. “We’ve got pictures of a raccoon and a cat sharing the same food bowl, side by side.” By Lisa L. Yet the disease is almost entirely preventable if exposed individuals receive timely post-exposure prophylaxis, a regimen of vaccination and, in higher-risk cases, immunoglobulin administration that can stop the virus before it reaches the nervous system. A new retrospective study from Hangzhou, China, published in BMC Infectious Diseases, has now added an important piece to the puzzle of why some people fail to access this lifesaving care promptly, and the answer points squarely at age. Researchers led by Zheng Yang of the Emergency Department at Tongde Hospital of Zhejiang Province, affiliated with Zhejiang Chinese Medical University, analyzed 3,327 exposure-related clinic presentations recorded between October 2022 and October 2025. The team began with a larger pool of records and applied rigorous exclusion criteria, removing seven system-test entries, fifteen exposures classified as World Health Organization Category I, thirteen confirmed continuation visits, ten records with contradictory dates, and two unresolved duplicates. What remained was a clean hospital-based cohort suitable for examining two distinct questions: how quickly patients presented after a potential rabies exposure, and whether they had attempted any wound care on their own before arriving at the clinic. The central finding concerns timing. Of the 3,327 presentations, 218, or 6.6 percent, occurred on a calendar day after the day of injury. Because the study relied on electronic medical records rather than precise timestamps, the researchers used a date-based operational proxy for delay: presenting on a subsequent calendar day rather than the same day. This is a conservative measure, and the authors are careful to frame it as such, but it captures a meaningful gap in access to care. Rabies virus travels along peripheral nerves at a relatively slow rate, and every hour of delay before prophylaxis begins extends the window during which the virus could, in principle, establish itself at the wound site and begin its ascent. When the researchers fitted multivariable logistic regression models adjusting for other characteristics, patients aged 65 and older had significantly higher adjusted odds of subsequent-calendar-day presentation compared with the reference group aged 15 to 44 years. The adjusted odds ratio was 2.28, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 1.31 to 3.96 and a P value of 0.003. In practical terms, older adults in this cohort were more than twice as likely to show up at the clinic only after the calendar day of their exposure had passed. This age-related pattern persisted even after accounting for other variables in the model, suggesting that advancing age itself, or factors closely tied to it, creates a genuine barrier to prompt care-seeking after an animal bite or scratch. The study also examined pre-hospital wound management, the self-directed cleaning or treatment that patients perform before reaching professional care. Guidelines from the World Health Organization emphasize immediate and thorough washing of bite wounds with soap and running water for at least fifteen minutes, a simple intervention that mechanically reduces viral load at the exposure site. The researchers modeled any pre-hospital wound self-treatment as a separate binary outcome. Interestingly, the estimate for the oldest age group pointed in the opposite direction: patients aged 65 and older appeared less likely to report any self-treatment, with an adjusted odds ratio of 0.71 and a confidence interval of 0.50 to 1.01. However, this estimate did not reach the conventional threshold of statistical significance, with a P value of 0.056, and the authors explicitly caution that it is imprecise and requires confirmation in future work. A methodologically important point in the paper is that the two outcomes were modeled separately. The authors stress that their analysis does not establish a combined individual-level outcome linking delay and self-treatment within the same patient. In other words, the data cannot tell us whether an older adult who delays presentation is also the same person who skips wound washing, or whether these behaviors occur independently across the cohort. This distinction matters for intervention design: if delay and inadequate wound care cluster in the same individuals, targeted outreach could address both at once, whereas independent patterns might require broader, population-level messaging. Two other associations emerged from the models. Patients who reported any pre-hospital wound self-treatment had higher adjusted odds of subsequent-calendar-day presentation, with an adjusted odds ratio of 2.72 and a 95 percent confidence interval of 2.00 to 3.69. One plausible interpretation is that people who attempt self-care may believe they have managed the problem adequately and therefore postpone professional evaluation, though the observational design of the study prevents any firm causal claim. The temporal pattern of the data also revealed that presentations during the clinic-opening calendar period of October through December 2022 were associated with subsequent-calendar-day presentation, with an adjusted odds ratio of 2.54. The authors interpret this finding as exploratory, noting that it may reflect the establishment phase of the clinic itself, shifts in case mix, seasonality of animal exposures, or unmeasured access factors rather than any stable behavioral pattern. The implications for rabies control programs, particularly in China where dog-mediated rabies persists at low but nonzero levels, are significant. Older adults represent a vulnerable population on multiple fronts. They may have reduced mobility, limited awareness of modern PEP protocols, greater reliance on traditional remedies, or fewer social contacts who can urge them to seek care quickly. Sensory and cognitive changes can also affect how seriously a minor bite wound is perceived. Because the incubation period of rabies can range from weeks to months depending on the site and severity of exposure, a delay of even one day is unlikely to be decisive in every case, but the cumulative effect of late presentation across a population contributes to preventable deaths. Public health campaigns that specifically target older adults, perhaps through community health workers, primary care touchpoints, or family-centered messaging, could help close this gap. The study’s design has limitations that the authors acknowledge. As a retrospective, single-center, hospital-based analysis, it captures only people who eventually reached the clinic, leaving unexamined the experiences of exposed individuals who never sought care at all. The date-based proxy for delay is coarser than exact time-to-presentation measurements, and self-reported wound treatment is subject to recall bias. The clinic-opening period association is explicitly flagged as potentially confounded by factors the data cannot disentangle. Nevertheless, the large cohort size, careful data cleaning, and transparent statistical reporting give the findings credibility, and the consistency of the age effect with prior studies cited in the paper’s supplementary comparisons, including work from Hangzhou and Wuhan, strengthens the case that delayed presentation among older adults is a reproducible phenomenon rather than a local artifact. Funded by the Zhejiang Provincial Bureau of Disease Control and Prevention Science and Technology Program, the study received ethics approval from Tongde Hospital of Zhejiang Province and was conducted on de-identified electronic medical record data with a waiver of informed consent, in accordance with the 2013 Declaration of Helsinki. As rabies continues to kill an estimated tens of thousands of people worldwide each year, most of them in Asia and Africa, research of this kind translates a grim global statistic into actionable local insight. The message for clinicians and health communicators is clear: when it comes to rabies post-exposure prophylaxis, age is not just a demographic variable but a risk factor for the behaviors that allow a preventable disease to claim lives. Ensuring that older adults recognize exposures as emergencies, wash wounds immediately, and reach prophylaxis clinics without delay may prove one of the most cost-effective interventions available in the ongoing effort to eliminate rabies deaths. Policy Diversity, Equity and Inclusion FY25 Impact Report 2022-2026 Strategic Plan WYSO Station Updates Local & Statewide News Clark County reports human cases of West Nile, animal case of rabies WYSO | By Shay Frank Published October 1, 2026 at 2:26 PM EDT Facebook LinkedIn Email CDC / Public Domain Mosquitoes spread the West Nile virus. Clark County is investigating two infectious diseases including a human case of West Nile virus and a case of rabies in a bat. The human West Nile virus case is on the southern side of Elmwood Place in Springfield, while the rabid bat was found in the village of Medway in Bethel Township. Both cases of infectious disease are making their first appearance since 2021 in the county. West Nile virus is spread by infected mosquitoes that bite humans and rabies can be transmitted to humans by a variety of animals. Bats are the most common carriers of rabies and the only animals who have tested positive for rabies in Clark County in the last 20 years. West Nile virus cannot spread from person to person. The illness spread by mosquito also often goes undetected as 80% of infected people show no symptoms. If symptoms do show up for those exposed, they typically onset within three to fourteen days. Those include severe or mild fever, inflammation of the brain, head and body aches, vomiting, diarrhea, rash and swollen glands. Mild symptoms can last for a few days to a week. The Clark County Combined Health District said the best way to protect yourself is to prevent mosquito bites with EPA registered insect repellent. When outdoors, residents are encouraged to also wear loose-fitting, long sleeves and pants to protect from exposure. Residents can also prevent mosquitos around their home by emptying or covering items that hold water like buckets, tires, flowerpots, birdbaths and trash containers. If they cannot be emptied or discarded, residents can use products containing Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis to control mosquito larvae. the product is available at many garden and home improvement stores, About one in 150 people infected with the virus develop severe illness. Those symptoms include as high fever, headache, neck stiffness, muscle weakness, disorientation, tremors, seizures, paralysis, and coma. For rabies, exposure can come from a bite, scratch, direct skin contact with an infected animal and even sharing a room with that animal. Pet owners are encouraged to vaccinate their dogs and cats for rabies and keep domestic animals clear of all wildlife. If a bat is found near an unattended child or someone unable to communicate if exposure has occurred, exposure may have still happened. The resident who discovered the infected bat in Clark County has received life-saving post exposure prophylaxis. While rabies is rare in humans, it is always fatal once symptoms arise. If exposure has happened immediate medical care is critical. Officials said it is always best to capture the bat for testing but not to touch it with bare hands. People and pets should be kept away from the animal and doors or windows should be closed to limit escape. Once a bat is found and captured, residents should contact Clark County Health for guidance on testing it for rabies. The health department can be reached at 937-390-5600 or at info@clarkhealthohio.gov.
